title: Why does the north have summer when Earth is farthest from the Sun?
answer: The tilt of Earth’s axis, not its distance from the Sun, makes the seasons

checks.question: At the December solstice London’s noon Sun gives 26% of overhead sunlight at Earth’s average distance. Earth is then near its nearest point. Taking the distance into account, what share does London’s ground actually get?
checks.answer: About 27%. On the solstice Earth is about 0.984 of its average distance, so sunlight is about 3% stronger than average, and 26% × 1.03 is just under 27%: the distance adds one point to a share the tilt has cut from 88%.

checks.question: Suppose Earth’s axis kept its 23.44° tilt but swung round each year so that its north end always leaned toward the Sun. What would London get at the December solstice?
checks.answer: The same as in June: 16.4 h of daylight and 88% of overhead sunlight at noon. The real seasons swap because the axis keeps pointing the same way while Earth moves to the far side of the Sun; an axis that followed the Sun would keep London at its June values all year.

steps.title: Earth’s distance from the Sun changes through the year
steps.line: Predict: in which month is Earth nearest the Sun?
steps.caption: Earth’s orbit is slightly oval, so it passes nearest the Sun once a year and farthest half a year later. A common guess is that the seasons follow this distance, with summer when Earth is nearest. The oval is drawn far more stretched than it is.
steps.picture: An exaggerated oval orbit with the Sun off centre: Earth nearest the Sun at one end and farthest at the other, each asking which month.

steps.title: Nearest the Sun in early January, while the north tilts away
steps.line: Predict: in June, does Tromsø get more or less than 12 hours of daylight?
steps.caption: Earth is nearest the Sun in early January, when the north has winter and the south summer. Distance cannot explain opposite seasons at once. The tilt of Earth’s axis, not its distance from the Sun, makes the seasons: the tilted axis keeps pointing the same way, so the north leans sunward in June and away in December. Sizes and distances are not to scale.
steps.picture: An orbit around the Sun, not to scale; Earth in June (right), September (top), December (left) and March (bottom), its axis tilted the same way each time; Beside December’s Earth: nearest the Sun in early January.

steps.title: Tromsø in June: 24.0 h of daylight, noon Sun at 43.8°
steps.line: Red dot: Tromsø; yellow: its daylight, along its line.
steps.caption: In June the north end leans toward the Sun far enough that Tromsø’s whole latitude circle sits on the day side. As Earth turns, Tromsø never enters the night half, so the Sun stays up for all 24 hours. At noon in June the Sun is overhead at 23.44° N; that latitude is the Sun’s declination, and through the year it moves between 23.44° N and 23.44° S.
steps.picture: The Sun, not to scale; Earth in June from the side, Tromsø’s latitude circle yellow where lit; June’s noon Sun ray, 43.8° above Tromsø’s horizon; 1 label.

steps.title: June noon: the Sun stands 43.8° up, giving 69% of overhead sunlight per m²
steps.line: Yellow: one beam, spread across the ground; white: the horizon.
steps.caption: The white line is Tromsø’s horizon. A lower Sun spreads the same beam over more ground, sharing its light across a larger patch. A higher Sun concentrates that light. Here each square metre receives 69% of what it would under an overhead Sun, before the air takes its share. The noon Sun’s height is 90° minus the distance from Tromsø’s latitude to the declination: 90° − |69.65° − 23.44°| = 43.79°.
steps.picture: Earth in June from the side, Tromsø’s latitude circle yellow where lit; June’s noon Sun ray, 43.8° above Tromsø’s horizon; Close-up on Tromsø at noon in June: its horizon, the noon sunlight, and the 43.8° angle between them, 90° − |69.65° − 23.44°| = 43.79°. A yellow beam lands on a patch of horizon 1.45 times its width: per m² of ground, sin 43.8° = 0.69 of overhead sunlight. New in this step: Close-up on Tromsø at noon in June: its horizon, the noon sunlight, and the 43.8° angle between them, 90° − |69.65° − 23.44°| = 43.79°. A yellow beam lands on a patch of horizon 1.45 times its width: per m² of ground, sin 43.8° = 0.69 of overhead sunlight.

steps.title: December: the same axis, and Tromsø’s daylight goes 24.0 h to 0.0 h
steps.line: Predict: of Tromsø, London, Quito and Sydney, whose daylight changes most?
steps.caption: Half an orbit later Earth is on the far side of the Sun, but the axis still points the same way, so the south end now leans sunward and the hemispheres swap seasons. Tromsø’s daylight falls to 0.0 h. Its noon Sun stays below the horizon, so it gets no direct sunlight. Both the longer days and the stronger sunlight fall in June, so Tromsø receives the most sunlight around then.
steps.picture: The Sun, not to scale; Earth in June from the side, Tromsø’s latitude circle yellow where lit; June’s noon Sun ray, 43.8° above Tromsø’s horizon; Earth in December from the side, Tromsø’s latitude circle yellow where lit; December’s noon Sun ray, stopped by the globe: below Tromsø’s horizon; June on the right; December on the left; 4 labels. steps.title: The same 1 m beam lands on 1.45 m of ground in June; in December the noon Sun is down
steps.line: Both noon beams on level ground at Tromsø, drawn to one scale.
steps.caption: Here the noon sunlight from both globes lands on level ground at Tromsø. Each beam is 1 m across, measured at right angles to its rays. June’s Sun, 43.8° up, lays its beam on 1.45 m of ground, so each square metre gets 1 ÷ 1.45 = 69% of what an overhead Sun gives. In December the noon Sun stays 3.1° below the horizon, so no beam reaches the ground.

steps.title: Tromsø swings from 24.0 h to 0.0 h; Quito stays at 12.0 h
steps.line: Yellow: the lit part of each circle, which latitude sets.
steps.caption: Each line follows one place as Earth turns; yellow marks the daylight part. Tromsø’s circle is all day in June and all night in December, while the equator’s is always cut in half. London and Sydney sit between those extremes. These ideal day lengths count the Sun’s centre above a flat horizon, leaving out atmospheric bending and local terrain.

steps.title: Tromsø’s daylight through the year
steps.line: By the model, 24 h for 60 days and 0 h for 61; an almanac’s polar night is shorter.
steps.caption: The curve runs the same model through the year. It stays flat at 24 hours for 60 days around the June solstice, the span the dimension marks, when Tromsø’s whole circle is lit, and at 0 for 61 days around December; the flat parts represent continuous daylight or darkness, rather than a pause in Earth’s rotation. Earth is nearest the Sun in early January, two weeks after the December solstice.
steps.picture: A chart of daylight in hours, 0 to 24, through the months January to December; Tromsø’s daylight through the year, from 0.0 h to 24.0 h, flat at 24 h for 60 days and at 0 h for 61; Dashed lines at the March and September equinoxes and the June and December solstices; The curve’s value on those days: Mar equinox 12.0 h, Jun solstice 24.0 h, Sep equinox 12.0 h, Dec solstice 0.0 h; A dimension line marked “60 days”; 1 label.

steps.title: 15 January: 0.0 h of daylight in Tromsø, 24.0 h at 69.7° S
steps.line: Purple: the same model at 69.7° S. The bars set the two causes side by side.
steps.caption: Back to the opening question. Distance still changes incoming sunlight: an equally oriented surface receives about 7% more in January than in July, before atmospheric absorption. Both hemispheres share this distance change. The tilt moves Tromsø’s noon sunlight between 0% and 69% of overhead. On 15 January Tromsø gets 0.0 h of daylight and 69.7° S, the purple curve, gets 24.0 h; both are the same distance from the Sun that day, so the gap between them comes from the tilt.

steps.title: Earth’s distance from the Sun changes through the year
steps.line: Predict: in which month is Earth nearest the Sun?
steps.caption: Earth’s orbit is slightly oval, so it passes nearest the Sun once a year and farthest half a year later. A common guess is that the seasons follow this distance, with summer when Earth is nearest. The oval is drawn far more stretched than it is.
steps.picture: An exaggerated oval orbit with the Sun off centre: Earth nearest the Sun at one end and farthest at the other, each asking which month.

steps.title: Nearest the Sun in early January, while the north tilts away
steps.line: Predict: in June, does Sydney get more or less than 12 hours of daylight?
steps.caption: Earth is nearest the Sun in early January, when the north has winter and the south summer. Distance cannot explain opposite seasons at once. The tilt of Earth’s axis, not its distance from the Sun, makes the seasons: the tilted axis keeps pointing the same way, so the north leans sunward in June and away in December. Sizes and distances are not to scale.
steps.picture: An orbit around the Sun, not to scale; Earth in June (right), September (top), December (left) and March (bottom), its axis tilted the same way each time; Beside December’s Earth: nearest the Sun in early January.

steps.title: Sydney in June: 9.7 h of daylight, noon Sun at 32.7°
steps.line: Red dot: Sydney; yellow: its daylight, along its line.
steps.caption: In June the north end of the axis leans toward the Sun. Sydney is south of the equator, so its noon Sun is low and most of its latitude circle, the line through the dot, is on the night side: 9.7 h of daylight in its winter. At noon in June the Sun is overhead at 23.44° N; that latitude is the Sun’s declination, and through the year it moves between 23.44° N and 23.44° S.
steps.picture: The Sun, not to scale; Earth in June from the side, Sydney’s latitude circle yellow where lit; June’s noon Sun ray, 32.7° above Sydney’s horizon; 1 label.

steps.title: June noon: the Sun stands 32.7° up, giving 54% of overhead sunlight per m²
steps.line: Yellow: one beam, spread across the ground; white: the horizon.
steps.caption: The white line is Sydney’s horizon. A lower Sun spreads the same beam over more ground, sharing its light across a larger patch. A higher Sun concentrates that light. Here each square metre receives 54% of what it would under an overhead Sun, before the air takes its share. The noon Sun’s height is 90° minus the distance from Sydney’s latitude to the declination: 90° − |-33.87° − 23.44°| = 32.69°.
steps.picture: Earth in June from the side, Sydney’s latitude circle yellow where lit; June’s noon Sun ray, 32.7° above Sydney’s horizon; Close-up on Sydney at noon in June: its horizon, the noon sunlight, and the 32.7° angle between them, 90° − |-33.87° − 23.44°| = 32.69°. A yellow beam lands on a patch of horizon 1.85 times its width: per m² of ground, sin 32.7° = 0.54 of overhead sunlight. New in this step: Close-up on Sydney at noon in June: its horizon, the noon sunlight, and the 32.7° angle between them, 90° − |-33.87° − 23.44°| = 32.69°. A yellow beam lands on a patch of horizon 1.85 times its width: per m² of ground, sin 32.7° = 0.54 of overhead sunlight.

steps.title: December: the same axis, and Sydney’s daylight goes 9.7 h to 14.3 h
steps.line: Predict: of Tromsø, London, Quito and Sydney, whose daylight changes most?
steps.caption: Half an orbit later Earth is on the far side of the Sun, but the axis still points the same way, so the south end now leans sunward and the hemispheres swap seasons. Sydney’s daylight rises to 14.3 h. Its noon Sun is higher, 79.6° up, concentrating the beam over less ground: 98% of overhead sunlight per m², against 54% in June. Both the longer days and the stronger sunlight fall in December, so Sydney receives the most sunlight around then.
steps.picture: The Sun, not to scale; Earth in June from the side, Sydney’s latitude circle yellow where lit; June’s noon Sun ray, 32.7° above Sydney’s horizon; Earth in December from the side, Sydney’s latitude circle yellow where lit; December’s noon Sun ray, 79.6° above Sydney’s horizon; June on the right; December on the left; 4 labels. New in this step: The Sun, not to scale; Earth in December from the side, Sydney’s latitude circle yellow where lit; December’s noon Sun ray, 79.6° above Sydney’s horizon; and 2 more.

steps.title: The same 1 m beam lands on 1.85 m of ground in June, 1.02 m in December
steps.line: Both noon beams on level ground at Sydney, drawn to one scale.
steps.caption: Here the noon sunlight from both globes lands on level ground at Sydney. Each beam is 1 m across, measured at right angles to its rays. June’s Sun, 32.7° up, lays its beam on 1.85 m of ground, so each square metre gets 1 ÷ 1.85 = 54% of what an overhead Sun gives. December’s Sun, 79.6° up, lays its beam on 1.02 m of ground, so each square metre gets 1 ÷ 1.02 = 98% of what an overhead Sun gives. Counted at Earth’s average distance, as the percentages are, both beams carry the same sunlight; June’s spreads it over 1.8 times as much ground as December’s, which is how 98% per m² falls to 54%.
steps.picture: The Sun, not to scale; Earth in June from the side, Sydney’s latitude circle yellow where lit; June’s noon Sun ray, 32.7° above Sydney’s horizon; Earth in December from the side, Sydney’s latitude circle yellow where lit; December’s noon Sun ray, 79.6° above Sydney’s horizon; June on the right; December on the left; Level ground at Sydney, with both noon beams drawn to one scale, each 1 m across: June’s, at 32.7°, lands on 1.85 m, 54% per m²; December’s, at 79.6°, lands on 1.02 m, 98% per m². New in this step: Level ground at Sydney, with both noon beams drawn to one scale, each 1 m across: June’s, at 32.7°, lands on 1.85 m, 54% per m²; December’s, at 79.6°, lands on 1.02 m, 98% per m².

steps.title: Tromsø swings from 24.0 h to 0.0 h; Quito stays at 12.0 h
steps.line: Yellow: the lit part of each circle, which latitude sets.
steps.caption: Each line follows one place as Earth turns; yellow marks the daylight part. Tromsø’s circle is all day in June and all night in December, while the equator’s is always cut in half. London and Sydney sit between those extremes. These ideal day lengths count the Sun’s centre above a flat horizon, leaving out atmospheric bending and local terrain.
steps.picture: The Sun, not to scale; Earth in June from the side, Sydney’s latitude circle yellow where lit; June’s noon Sun ray, 32.7° above Sydney’s horizon; Earth in December from the side, Sydney’s latitude circle yellow where lit; December’s noon Sun ray, 79.6° above Sydney’s horizon; June on the right; December on the left; The other places’ latitude circles on both views, yellow where lit; “June”, 4 labelled values; “December”, 4 labelled values. Marked: Sydney: 9.7 h; Sydney: 14.3 h. New in this step: The other places’ latitude circles on both views, yellow where lit; “June”, 4 labelled values; “December”, 4 labelled values.

steps.title: Sydney’s daylight through the year
steps.line: Shortest 9.7 h in June, longest 14.3 h in December.
steps.caption: The curve runs the same model through the year. Sydney’s curve is upside down from a northern one: its shortest day, 9.7 h, falls at the June solstice and its longest, 14.3 h, in December. The dimension on the right measures the gap, 4.6 h. Earth is nearest the Sun in early January, two weeks after the December solstice.
steps.picture: A chart of daylight in hours, 0 to 24, through the months January to December; Sydney’s daylight through the year, from 9.7 h to 14.3 h; Dashed lines at the March and September equinoxes and the June and December solstices; The curve’s value on those days: Mar equinox 12.0 h, Jun solstice 9.7 h, Sep equinox 12.0 h, Dec solstice 14.3 h; Dashed lines from the shortest day, 9.7 h, and the longest, 14.3 h, to the right of the chart; A dimension line marked “longest − shortest: 4.6 h”.

steps.title: 15 January: 14.0 h of daylight in Sydney, 10.0 h at 33.9° N
steps.line: Purple: the same model at 33.9° N. The bars set the two causes side by side.
steps.caption: Back to the opening question. Distance still changes incoming sunlight: an equally oriented surface receives about 7% more in January than in July, before atmospheric absorption. Both hemispheres share this distance change. The tilt moves Sydney’s noon sunlight between 54% and 98% of overhead. On 15 January Sydney gets 14.0 h of daylight and 33.9° N, the purple curve, gets 10.0 h; both are the same distance from the Sun that day, so the gap between them comes from the tilt.
